title: The clever steward (Luke 16:1–13)
hookLine: a crooked manager is praised for being shrewd; you can't serve God and mammon

lines: A PARABLE READERS STILL ARGUE ABOUT.
cards: A manager is caught wasting his boss's money. He's about to be fired. So he spends his last afternoon cooking the books in his customers' favor.
And at the end of the story, the boss praises him. This is a parable preachers sometimes approach carefully, and readers still argue about parts of it. It sounds like Jesus is applauding fraud.
He isn't. To see what he is doing, watch the manager's hands.

teach.b: A rich man hears his steward has wasted his goods. He calls him in: give an account, you're done. The steward thinks fast.
I can't dig, I'm ashamed to beg. I know what I'll do, so that people will take me into their homes. He calls in his master's debtors one by one.
A hundred barrels of oil. Sit down quickly, write fifty. And you?
A hundred quarters of wheat. Write eighty. He's making friends with the only currency he has left.
Then the surprise: "And the lord commended the unjust steward, forasmuch as he had done wisely: for the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light."

teach.h: PRAISED FOR SEEING THE END COMING.
teach.b: Notice what's praised. Not the dishonesty; he's still called unjust. He saw the end coming and acted.
He knew his position wouldn't last, and he used what was passing through his hands to make friends who would.

teach.h: WHEN YOU FAIL, FRIENDS RECEIVE YOU.
teach.b: Jesus draws the lesson: make friends with the mammon of iniquity, so that when you fail, when your own time runs out, they may receive you into everlasting dwellings.

Mammon is the Douay's word for wealth, money and property. In the Catholic reading, everyone is a steward like this one, who will one day be asked to give an account. So use it now, while it's in your hands, for people.

teach.h: YOU CANNOT SERVE GOD AND MAMMON.
teach.b: Then the line the passage ends on: "You cannot serve God and mammon." No servant can serve two masters.

how: Catholics often speak of stewardship, the idea that time, talent and money are entrusted by God rather than owned outright, and some parishes ask members to make an annual stewardship commitment.

o: a coin used to pay the Temple tax
the steward's cruel and greedy boss
wealth and property, a rival master

games.q: the clever steward — tap the pairs.
p: Aramaic: wealth that people trust in

s: Jesus praises the steward for cheating
he's still called unjust. he's praised for seeing the end coming and acting wisely.
the steward cut the debts to make friends who would take him in
he used what passed through his hands to make lasting friends.
mammon is the name of a demon in Luke's Gospel
in Luke it means wealth, set beside God as a master someone could serve.

games.q: you're the steward. you're fired, and you have one afternoon left with the books. what do you do?
o: beg the master for one more chance.
call in the debtors and cut their bills.
quietly take some money for yourself.
games.why: he cuts their debts so they'll welcome him later. the master commends him for acting wisely, though he's still called unjust.

practice: Picture what's passing through your hands this week, a paycheck, an allowance, a budget, even a few dollars, and notice that none of it stays.
Think of one person you could do some good for with a small part of it: a coworker's lunch, a friend's coffee, a family that's struggling. If you pray, ask to be a faithful steward.

wordCard.voice: Mammon. The Douay's word for wealth, money and property, what the crooked steward used to make friends before his time ran out. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from Aramaic mamona: wealth, property, what a person trusts in.

carryVoice: Your line: god or mammon. What you hold, you won't hold forever. That's day four hundred seventy-one.

sources.q: And the lord commended the unjust steward, forasmuch as he had done wisely: for the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light.
You cannot serve God and mammon.
